title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release-note highlights, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki pointers. It is intended for engineers (runtime, infra, SRE) and solutions/SEs onboarding heavy inference workloads.

Goals
- Describe the architecture and key components that deliver low-latency, high-throughput LLM inference.
- Capture the kernel scheduling model and execution policies used in production.
- Provide an actionable profiling playbook and benchmarking suite to reproduce performance numbers.
- Give concise runbooks for common incidents (latency spikes, OOMs, degraded throughput).
- Maintain a single-team wiki reference for ownership, contacts, and release notes.

Runtime architecture (high-level)

The runtime is composed of these logical layers:

1) Ingress / API Frontend
- Responsible for authentication, quota checks, request validation, and routing.
- Route decisions consider model compatibility, region, customer tier, and availability.

2) Smart Router / Orchestrator
- Maintains global view of capacity and model variants.
- Implements policy-based routing (latency-first, cost-first, fallback to smaller model variant).
- Performs request batching windows for compatible requests.

3) Serving Nodes (GPU workers)
- Host model replicas; each node runs multiple serving processes with per-process kernel contexts.
- Responsible for KV-cache management, sequence cache (per-session), and kernel-level memory pools.

4) Kernel Execution Layer
- Optimized kernels (attention, matmul, softmax) are selected dynamically per model/shard.
- Runtime supports multiple backends: cuBLAS/cuDNN, Triton-optimized kernels, custom CUDA fused kernels, and CPU fallbacks.

5) Telemetry & Observability
- Traces, per-token metrics, kernel-level counters, and resource metrics are exported to observability stack.
- Perf dashboards expose token/sec, GPU-util, mem-pressure, scheduling-queue-length, and batch sizes.

Key architectural patterns
- Continuous batching (adaptive): micro-batching windows vary by workload to balance latency vs cost.
- Prefix / KV caching: warm prefixes skip compute for cached KV context.
- Quantization-aware execution: different kernel paths for float16/int8/4-bit kernels.
- Preemption-friendly tasks: short running control-plane ops can preempt non-critical background maintenance.

Kernel scheduling design

Objectives
- Maximize GPU utilization while meeting SLOs (p50/p95/p99 latencies and token throughput).
- Avoid head-of-line blocking caused by large-sequence requests.
- Gracefully handle mixed batch shapes and model families.

Scheduling primitives and concepts
- Slots: a GPU is partitioned into logical slots representing concurrent kernel streams with isolated memory arenas.
- Priority classes: interactive (high), background (low), batch-async (medium).
- Work-stealing: idle slots pull pending micro-batches from other slots within node to improve throughput.
- Admission control: requests are admitted into batching window if expected latency impact is within threshold.

Scheduling algorithm (summary)
1. Incoming request classified by priority and expected tokens.
2. Router computes candidate nodes based on affinity (model shard locality, kv-cache warmness).
3. If candidate nodes have an open slot, request is enqueued into slot's micro-batcher.
4. Micro-batcher triggers execution when either batch timeout (adaptive; default 6ms for interactive) or max batch size reached.
5. Large-sequence requests (> 1024 tokens baseline) are routed to dedicated large-seq pools with longer batching windows.
6. On kernel launch, scheduler uses a kernel-selection heuristic: choose fused/custom kernel if input shapes and quantization mode match; otherwise fallback to generic path.

Preemption & fairness
- Short preemption windows (target 1ms) allow high-priority interactive jobs to bump long-running background kernels.
- Fairness policy ensures no tenant can monopolize slots beyond configured max_concurrency.
- Metrics: preemption_count, preemption_latency_ms, preemption_fallbacks monitor preemption health.

Memory management and OOM mitigation
- Per-slot memory arenas allocated from a global GPU pool.
- Eviction policies: stale kv-cache segments and inactive sessions are reclaimed first.
- OOM path: fail-fast for non-critical background work, attempt soft-fallback to quantized kernel, last-resort signals to router to spill to other nodes.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

This section explains how to reproduce, profile, and triage performance regressions. Follow these steps on a staging cluster before running in prod.

1) Reproduce the baseline
- Use the benchmark harness (see Benchmarking suite) with representative prompts and the same model/config as production.
- Capture the failing trace window (10–30 minutes) and include request IDs for trace correlation.

2) Collect metrics and traces
- Collect distributed traces (header X-Trace-Id) and kube/pod metrics.
- Commands:
  - kubectl -n runtime logs -l app=serving-node --since=10m | grep "TRACE_ID=<id>"
  - perf tool: runtime-profiler record --trace-id <id> --duration 60s --output /tmp/profile.pb

3) Lightweight profiling (online)
- Check batch sizes and batching latency: query /metrics on the serving node (prometheus endpoints):
  - batch_size_histogram, batch_latency_ms_bucket, queue_length_gauge
- Check kernel-level counters exposed by the CUDA profiler metric exporter:
  - sm_efficiency, achieved_occupancy, total_mem_bw_util

4) Deep profiling (off-host)
- Run a sampled CUDA nvprof or Nsight capture on a replica:
  - nsight-sys --trace=cuda --duration 30s --output /tmp/trace.qdrep
  - Use nvtx ranges added by the runtime to map sections to code paths.

5) Kernel selection debugging
- Enable kernel-selection debug logs: runtime-config set --node <id> --log-kernel-selection true
- Re-run a small test and inspect logs to confirm the chosen kernel path and fallback reasons.

6) Memory analysis
- Dump allocator stats: runtime-admin dump-alloc --node <id> --out /tmp/alloc.json
- Look for fragmentation (>30% lost-to-frag) or multiple large allocations causing OOM.

7) Action and mitigation
- If small batches and high kernel latency: analyze kernel occupancy and consider switching to a more fused kernel or recompiling kernels for target shapes.
- If queue_length grows: increase slot count or scale replica count; for short-term remediation, change routing policy to route to warm nodes only.
- If OOM: reduce max_concurrency, evict kv-caches, or move request to a large-seq node pool.

Benchmarking suite

Purpose: reproducible harness for end-to-end latency and throughput tests. Suite components:
- benchmark-runner (CLI harness)
- model-workloads repo (sets of prompts, user-pattern traces)
- perf-configs (YAML configs for concurrency, seq-lengths, qps profiles)
- golden-results (historical baselines)

Example perf config (YAML)

name: chat-short-llama-13b
model: redwood/llama-13b-v2
quantization: int8
concurrency: 128
qps_profile: bursty-1m
sequence_length: 32
duration_minutes: 30
metrics: [latency_p50, latency_p95, latency_p99, tokens_per_second, gpu_util]

Running a benchmark (example)
- benchmark-runner run --config perf-configs/chat-short-llama-13b.yaml --target-cluster staging --out /tmp/results.json
- After run: benchmark-analyzer compare --actual /tmp/results.json --golden golden-results/chat-short-llama-13b-2027-09-01.json

Fail criteria and CI gating
- Latency regressions: increases in p95 > 10% or p99 > 5% relative to golden fail CI.
- Throughput regressions: tokens/sec decrease > 7% fail CI.
- Any benchmark that exhibits >50% of runs with OOMs is auto-blocking.

Release notes (runtime highlights)

2027-11-15 (v3.9.2):
- Improved kernel-selection heuristic to prefer fused attention for common prompt shapes; p99 latency improved by ~8% on small-chat workloads.
- Added adaptive micro-batching default window reduction (from 8ms to 6ms) for interactive traffic.
- Memory arena fragmentation mitigation: new arena compaction path reduced peak mem by 12%.

2027-10-02 (v3.9.0):
- First stable release of preemption primitives with priority-classes and admission-control.
- Benchmarking suite integrated into CI for nightly regression checks.

Known issues (active)
- ISSUE-4179: Intermittent p99 spikes under bursty QPS on certain NVMe-backed nodes (root cause: I/O stall during KV cache checkpoint). Workaround: route high-QPS traffic to nodes with persistent-memory-backed caches. (Owner: eng-sre)
- ISSUE-3891: Rare OOM during long generation (>4096 tokens) when multiple large-session requests are colocated. Workaround: enable large-seq pool routing; set tenant max_concurrency for >=4096 token requests. (Owner: serving-runtime)
- ISSUE-4024: Nsight captures occasionally miss short-lived kernels due to sampling window; use repeated 10s captures as a workaround. (Owner: perf-team)

Operational runbooks (concise)

Runbook: High tail latency (p99) for interactive traffic
1. Confirm alert: alerts > p99_latency > 300ms for >5m (alerting rule).
2. Identify affected model(s) and nodes: query slow-traces service and filter by model name and trace tag.
3. Check metrics on nodes: batch_size_histogram (dropping to 1?), queue_length_gauge (growing?), gpu_util (low?).
4. If queue_length high and gpu_util low -> sign of head-of-line blocking. Actions:
   a) Add capacity (scale up replicas) or reroute to warm nodes.
   b) Temporarily increase priority of interactive class: runtime-admin set-priority interactive=high --node <id>
   c) If caused by a new release, rollback runtime image to previous stable tag.
5. If gpu_util high and kernel latency high -> profile kernels (see Profiling playbook) and escalate to perf-team.
6. Post-incident: run benchmark suite to capture regression and file a regression issue if needed.

Runbook: OOM on serving node
1. Alert: OOM event logged in node logs (OOM-kernel or cuda oom).
2. Actions:
   a) Drain node from router: router-admin drain-node <node-id> --reason "oom-investigation"
   b) Collect allocator dump: runtime-admin dump-alloc --node <node-id> --out /tmp/alloc.json
   c) Check recent deployments and config changes (max_concurrency, quantization toggles).
   d) If soft-retry possible, reduce max_concurrency and un-drain node once stable.
   e) If repeated OOMs, mark node for maintenance and redeploy with kernel memory tuning or upgraded GPU driver.

Runbook: Degraded throughput (tokens/sec drop)
1. Check cluster-wide QPS and compare to expected when golden tests ran.
2. Inspect network: packet drops, NVMe health, and PCIe errors.
3. Verify scheduler: increased preemption_count or high slot contention.
4. Remediation: increase shard parallelism or spin up more replicas, adjust batching windows.

Maintenance and change process
- Any kernel or scheduler change must be accompanied by:
  1) perf-run against golden workloads (benchmarks)
  2) canary rollout to < 5% traffic with increased tracing
  3) 48-hour post-deploy observation window before broad rollout
- Major memory allocator changes require a coordinated maintenance window and capacity headroom > 20%.

Appendix: useful commands
- runtime-admin list-nodes --filter "model=llama-13b"
- runtime-admin set-config --node <id> --key batching.window_ms --value 6
- benchmark-runner run --config perf-configs/chat-short-llama-13b.yaml --target-cluster staging

Appendix: exemplar observability queries
- Prometheus: rate(tokens_generated_total[1m]) by (node)
- Latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, model))
- Kernel occupancy: avg_over_time(cuda_kernel_occupancy[5m]) by (kernel_name)
